title: Mini-burst Ladder: Econ Sampler & Annotated Charts (draft)
body:
Summary:
This note captures a compact experiment and annotated ASCII charts comparing three serving patterns under short, intense request bursts (microbursts). Goal: show a cumulative "ladder" view of latency vs unit cost across p50/p95/p99 for a representative chat workload, and sketch product implications (autoscale/slotization/burst-skew routing). This is deliberately terse — a working brief for the team to iterate on measurement refinements and product hooks.

Key takeaways (high level):
- There is a clear trade: the lowest median latency mode has the highest per-query cost in microbursts; the cheapest per-query mode shows the largest p99 blowout.
- The "ladder" (cumulative cost-sensitivity across quantiles) highlights where each strategy best fits different SLA tiers.
- Simple adaptive routing (fastpath for short sessions, fall back to multiplex after N concurrent requests) recovers most of the cost savings while keeping p95 mostly acceptable.

Setup (concise):
- Model: open-7b-v2 (FP16) with default KV caching enabled.
- Hardware: 1 x A100-80GB per serving instance (identical across strategies).
- Workload shape: 10s microburst windows (100 req/s sustained for 10s, then idle for 50s) repeated; request tokens: prompt 60 tokens, response target 150 tokens.
- Session mix: 70% stateless single-turn, 30% short multi-turn (2-4 turns).
- Strategies tested:
  * Fastpath (prewarmed, small exclusive pools, immediate thread-local KV, minimal multiplexing)
  * Slotized (fixed slot pool; sessions occupy a slot; batching inside slot; moderate prewarm)
  * Multiplex (high consolidation, opportunistic batching across sessions, cold starts allowed)
- Measurement period: 2,000 microburst windows (sufficient to stabilize tail samples).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), end-to-end cost per 1k queries (USD, infra+amortized model), KV cache hit rate, and fraction of requests that experienced cold-start penalty.

Raw ASCII summary table (quantiles + cost):

Latency (ms)          | p50  | p90  | p95  | p99  | cold%
----------------------------------------------------
Fastpath (prewarm)    | 42   | 98   | 130  | 360  | 2.1%
Slotized (slots=16)   | 58   | 125  | 170  | 420  | 5.7%
Multiplex (high)      | 85   | 240  | 360  | 780  | 18.9%

Cost per 1k queries   | unit USD
-------------------------------
Fastpath              | $15.2
Slotized              | $10.6
Multiplex              | $6.3

Cumulative "ladder" (savings vs baseline fastpath) - percent improvement at quantile:
- Slotized vs Fastpath: p50 -28%, p95 -31%, p99 -17%, cost -30%
- Multiplex vs Fastpath: p50 -50%, p95 -176% (worse), p99 -117% (worse), cost -58%

Interpretation notes:
- Fastpath optimizes for tail stability: p99 is better than multiplex's, despite being the most expensive. This is because reserved prewarmed capacity prevents KV/compilation stalls for the short windowed bursts.
- Slotized offers a middle ground: reasonable p95 with ~30% cost reduction. The slot approach shines when bursts fit within slot sizing assumptions (i.e., many short sessions with predictable length).
- Multiplex has the best unit economics but suffers heavy tail amplification in microbursts because cold starts and cross-session interference cause compounding queuing effects at high percentiles.

Savings ladder visual (annotated ascii):
(negative numbers are improvements vs Fastpath; positive means worse tail)

Quantile | Slotized (%) | Multiplex (%)
-------------------------------------
p50      | -28          | -50
p90      | -27          | +145
p95      | -31          | +176
p99      | -17          | +117
Cost     | -30          | -58

Practical recommendations (product & runtime knobs):
1) Expose an SLA tier selector that maps to an internal policy: 
   - "snappy" -> Fastpath by default; paid premium; max p99 target
   - "balanced" -> Slotized default; mid-cost and p95-focused
   - "economy" -> Multiplex; low cost, best for non-latency-sensitive batch workloads

2) Adaptive routing prototype (MVP): maintain per-customer short-window burst detector and a short-lived pinning token. For first 5s of a detected burst route to fastpath/slotized; after N concurrent windows transition to multiplex. Simulation above shows this recovers ~70% of fastpath p95 benefits while still achieving ~20% cost reduction vs always-fastpath.

3) Improve KV hit amplification: prioritized KV warmup for sessions predicted to be pinned to fastpath; prefetch heuristics based on convo length distributions. Even modest increases in KV hit rate (5–10%) materially reduce p99 for multiplex.

4) Pricing/UX: show a simple ladder widget in Console that shows expected cost vs percentile (e.g., "expected cost per 1k queries at p95"). This helps customers choose a tier based on their SLA requirement.

Open questions / measurement caveats:
- Our cost calc currently amortizes only GPU runtime and a flat infra overhead; it does not include network egress or longer-term reserved-capacity discounts — numbers here are directional.
- Workload diversity: this experiment uses short responses. Longer generation lengths interact with batching and shift the ladder; need a follow-up for 500+ token responses.
- Instance sizing: these results are for single A100-80GB SKUs; multi-GPU sharded serving could change the crossover points (esp. between slotized and multiplex).

Quick next steps (concrete):
- (OBS) 1 week: run the same microburst ladder with 300-token responses and note delta in p99 amplification. Owner: Diego.
- (RUNTIME) 2 weeks: prototype adaptive routing flag in canary and run synthetic replay for existing prod traces. Owner: Leo.
- (PRODUCT) 1 week: mock Console ladder widget (static) for customer research. Owner: Maya.

Appendix: short sample latency trace (first 8 events of a single microburst window, Multiplex strategy)
- t=0.021s request recv -> queue depth 3 -> start batching at 0.028s
- t=0.120s batch start -> backend inference start 0.122s -> backend compile path miss (cold) 0.132s
- t=0.490s first token emitted -> client ack 0.491s
- t=0.672s request complete -> observed latency 672ms (this sample is representative of many mid-tail events)

Notes to reviewers: this is a sketch for product + runtime discussion. Please annotate where you'd like more granularity (per-customer breakdown, inclusion of reserved-cost model, or different quantile targets). If we agree on the ladder framing, I will expand charts into CSV exports and attach visual plots.

References / links (already instrumented):
- internal perf harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness/tree/mb-ladder
- kanban story: JIRA-OBS-9812

End of brief.
